{{short description|Set of guidelines for using statistical analysis}}
The '''MAGIC criteria''' are a set of guidelines put forth by [[Robert Abelson]] in his 1995 book ''Statistics as Principled Argument''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Abelson |first=Robert P. |url=http://archive.org/details/statisticsasprin0000abel |title=Statistics as principled argument |date=1995 |publisher=Hillsdale, N.J. : L. Erlbaum Associates |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-585-17659-8}}</ref> In this book he posits that the goal of statistical analysis should be to make compelling claims about the world<ref name = "jsvine">{{cite web|url=http://drafts.jsvine.com/the-magic-criteria/|title=The MAGIC Criteria|work=jsvine.com |accessdate=13 February 2020 |date=16 February 2015 }}</ref> and he presents the MAGIC criteria as a way to do that.

== What are the MAGIC criteria? ==

MAGIC is a [[backronym]] for:
# Magnitude – How big is the effect? Large effects are more compelling than small ones.
# Articulation – How specific is it?<ref name="sfu.ca">{{cite web |title=Criteria for a persuasive statistical argument: MAGIC |url=https://www2.cs.sfu.ca/CourseCentral/376/ted/376-08-1/MAGIC-criteria.pdf |website=COURSE HOME PAGE INDEX AND MAILLISTS |publisher=Simon Fraser University |accessdate=13 February 2020 |quote=Adapted from Abelson, Robert P. (1995). Statistics as principled argument. Hillsdale, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum, pp. 12–14.}}</ref> Precise statements are more compelling than imprecise ones. 
# Generality – How generally does it apply?<ref name = "jsvine"/> More general effects are more compelling than less general ones. Claims that would interest a more general audience are more compelling.<ref name="sfu.ca"/>
# Interestingness – interesting effects are those that "have the potential, through empirical analysis, to change what people believe about an important issue".<ref name = "jsvine"/>  More interesting effects are more compelling than less interesting ones. In addition, more surprising effects are more compelling than ones that merely confirm what is already known.<ref name="sfu.ca" />
# Credibility – Credible claims are more compelling than incredible ones. The researcher must show that the claims made are credible.<ref name = "jsvine"/> Results that contradict previously established ones are less credible.<ref name="sfu.ca" />

== Reviews and applications of the MAGIC criteria ==

Song Qian noted that the MAGIC criteria could be of use to ecologists.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Qian
 | first = Song
 | title = Statistics in ecology is for making a "principled argument"
 | journal = Landscape Ecology
 | volume = 29
 | pages = 937–939
 | date = 2014
 | issue = 6
 | issn =
 | doi = 10.1007/s10980-014-0042-y| doi-access = free
 }}</ref> Claudia Stanny discussed them in a course on psychology.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://uwf.edu/cstanny/website/ResearchDsgn/statistical%20claims%20abelson%201&2%20-%203%20slides.pdf|title=404 – Page Not Found {{!}} University of West Florida|last=Caludia|first=Stanny|date=|website=uwf.edu|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190416145254/http://uwf.edu/cstanny/website/ResearchDsgn/statistical%20claims%20abelson%201%262%20-%203%20slides.pdf|archive-date=2019-04-16|access-date=2019-12-23}}</ref> Anne Boomsma noted that they are useful when presenting results of complex statistical methods such as [[structural equation modelling]].<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Boomsma
 | first = Anne 
 | title = Reporting Analysis of Covariance Studies
 | journal = Structural Equation Modeling
 | volume = 7
 | pages = 461–483
 | date = 2000| doi = 10.1207/S15328007SEM0703_6

 }}</ref>
